extraReferences.title: Investigating body patterning in aquarium-raised flamboyant cuttlefish (Metasepia pfefferi). PeerJ 4: e2035
Color blindness and contrast perception in cuttlefish (Sepia officinalis) determined by a visual sensorimotor assay. Vision Research 46: 1746–1753
extraReferences.authors: Mäthger L.M., Barbosa A., Miner S., Hanlon R.T.

anatomy.lede: A flamboyant cuttlefish is a small, broad body with blade-like arms, fleshy flaps and a skin that never stops changing colour.

hotspots.label: Red arm tips
hotspots.text: The broad, blade-like arms carry four rows of suckers. Their tips often flush bright red, which may help ward off predators.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Like other cuttlefish, it is probably colour-blind, yet it can still produce colour patterns of great complexity.

hotspots.label: Papillae over the eye
hotspots.text: Fleshy papillae rise above the eyes, part of the skin texture it can raise and lower.

hotspots.label: Mantle flaps
hotspots.text: Three pairs of large, flat flaps stand up from the top of the very broad, oval mantle.

hotspots.label: Fin
hotspots.text: The fins edging the mantle pulse during its warning display, and help it 'walk' along the bottom together with its arms.

hotspots.label: Walking arms
hotspots.text: Two arms act like legs. Its cuttlebone is too small to keep it afloat for long, so it ambles over sand and mud instead of hovering.

senses.lede: Its senses are barely studied; what is known comes mostly from its better-known relatives.

senses.name: Colour-blind vision
senses.text: Tests on the common cuttlefish show that cuttlefish cannot tell colours apart, although they are sensitive to contrast. Researchers assume the flamboyant cuttlefish sees in the same way.

senses.name: A daytime hunter's eyes
senses.text: Unlike most cephalopods, it is active by day, when it can be seen hunting crustaceans and small fish in full light.

body.lede: Its body is built for walking rather than swimming, and for showing off rather than hiding.

systems.title: A cut-down cuttlebone
systems.text: The cuttlebone is a small rhombus, two-thirds to three-quarters the length of the mantle, and lacks the central ridge and outer cone found in most other cuttlefish.

systems.title: A skin of many parts
systems.text: In one aquarium study, researchers counted 7 texture, 14 posture and 7 movement components, plus 42–75 colour components, which combine into 11 distinct body patterns.

systems.title: Poisonous or not?
systems.text: Its muscle has been described as highly toxic, based on unpublished work. Preliminary later tests found only trace amounts of tetrodotoxin, too little to harm vertebrates.

mind.lede: Though described in 1885, this cuttlefish was not reported alive until 1988, and its behaviour is still poorly known.

studies.title: First seen alive
studies.text: The first report of living animals described an 'extremely rich' set of body-pattern components, but only as a preliminary inventory.

studies.title: Waves that never stop
studies.text: In five aquarium-bred adults, 8 of the 11 body patterns included waves of colour travelling across the mantle. In other cuttlefish such waves mostly appear during hunting, but these animals used them in many situations.

studies.title: Dark, not hidden
studies.text: Almost all the patterns recorded in the aquarium were dark, even over pale gravel, and the animals hardly tried to blend in. The authors suggest this may be a side effect of captivity, since wild animals are reported to camouflage well.

studies.title: Dens and duels
studies.text: Males fight over mating dens, and females visit a den to mate with the male living there.

survival.lede: Instead of fleeing, the flamboyant cuttlefish stands its ground and puts on a show.

tactics.title: Warning colours
tactics.text: When disturbed, it switches from its usual dark brown to black, dark brown and white with yellow patches, often with red arm tips.

tactics.title: An honest warning?
tactics.text: The display is often said to advertise poisonous flesh, but no significant toxin has yet been isolated, so what the warning protects remains unclear.

tactics.title: Camouflage on the hunt
tactics.text: It uses complex, changing camouflage to stalk its prey.

threats.title: Trawling and pollution
threats.text: Pollution, overfishing and habitat destruction threaten cephalopods like this one, and bottom trawling churns up the seafloor sediment it lives on.

life.lede: A flamboyant cuttlefish lives fast: it mates, lays a few eggs, and the female dies soon afterwards.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: Pairs mate face to face, and the male uses a special arm to pass a sperm packet into the female's mantle cavity.

stages.name: Eggs
stages.text: Eggs are laid singly in crevices or under ledges in coral, rock or wood; about a dozen were once found under half a coconut husk. Fresh eggs are white and slowly turn see-through.

stages.name: Hatchling
stages.text: Hatchlings are fully independent, receive no care, and can already make the same camouflage patterns as adults.

stages.name: End of life
stages.text: The female dies shortly after laying her eggs.
